tool.name: MahalanobisCovariance
tool.summary: Computes the mean vector, covariance matrix, inverse covariance matrix, and/or correlation matrix for a set of landscape variables and writes them as tables, for reuse by the Mahalanobis Raster and at Points tools through their Existing tables source.
tool.usage:
This tool calculates the multivariate statistics that the Mahalanobis distance formula D2 = (x - mu)' * Sigma^-1 * (x - mu) needs: the mean vector mu and the covariance matrix Sigma (and, optionally, the inverse covariance Sigma^-1 and the correlation matrix). It is the producer for the Mahalanobis suite - compute the mean and covariance once, then supply those two tables to the Mahalanobis Raster or at Points tools as their Existing tables source, so the statistics are not recomputed for every run.
The statistics are derived either from sample point features (the landscape variables are sampled at the points) or from the cells of a categorical raster that match a chosen value. The landscape variables are specified exactly as in the other Mahalanobis tools - one or more rasters (multiband rasters expand to one variable per band) plus optional polygon variables rasterized from a numeric field.
Each output table embeds the ordered variable list in its metadata, so when the tables are reused the consuming tool can verify that the same variables are supplied in the same order. Order matters: a different variable order silently produces incorrect distances.
Reference: Mahalanobis, P.C. (1936). On the generalised distance in statistics. Proceedings of the National Institute of Sciences of India 2(1):49-55.
Additional reading: Clark et al. (1993), Knick and Dyer (1997), and Farber and Kadmon (2002) illustrate Mahalanobis distances in ecological applications. For the underlying matrix algebra see Golub and Van Loan (1996), Meyer (2000), and Press et al. (2002).
Environments. This tool honors the Output Coordinate System, Cell Size, Processing Extent, Snap Raster, and Mask environments when aligning the landscape variables to a common analysis grid. Other geoprocessing environments do not affect it.

dialogReference.para: The raster datasets that define the multivariate space; their cell values are used (never any raster attribute-table values). At least one raster is required - it sets the analysis grid cell size, coordinate system, and extent.
A multiband raster is automatically expanded to one variable per band, named "raster_Band_X". To leave out specific bands, use the Bands to exclude table below.

Order matters: the variables become the columns of the mean vector and covariance matrix in the order listed (rasters first, then polygons). When you later reuse these tables in the Raster or at Points tools, supply the same datasets in the same order; a different order silently produces incorrect distances.

Optional polygon variables. Each row is a polygon feature class plus a numeric field, which is rasterized to the analysis grid using that field. Choose the field from the Numeric field dropdown. Polygon variables follow the raster variables in covariance-matrix order.

param.name: exclude_bands
param.displayname: Bands to exclude from multiband rasters (Optional)

dialogReference.para: Optional. To leave out specific bands of a multiband raster, add a row naming the multiband raster and the 1-based band number to exclude. Add one row for each band you want to drop.

How a raster value is read at a location that may not align to a cell center. Exact (nearest cell) uses the value of the cell the location falls in. Interpolated (bilinear) estimates the value from the four nearest cell centers.
This applies when sampling rasters at sample-point locations and when resampling rasters that do not already align to the analysis grid.

Exact cell values are more appropriate for categorical rasters, while bilinear interpolation is more appropriate for continuous rasters. Interpolation is rarely appropriate for categorical data unless the categories are at least ordinal, and preferably interval or ratio; it should never be used for nominal (unordered) categories.

param.name: stats_source
param.displayname: Source of mean vector and covariance matrix

dialogReference.para: Where the mean vector and covariance matrix are computed from.
Calculate directly from sample point features: sample the landscape variables at the supplied points and compute the statistics from those samples.
Categorical raster: compute the statistics from every cell of a categorical raster that equals a chosen value.
The Existing tables option is intentionally not offered here, because this tool produces those tables.

The reference point features whose locations define the sample used to build the statistics. Points falling outside the extent of any landscape raster, or on a NoData cell, are excluded and reported in the tool messages. Used only when the statistics source is sample point features.
If checked and the points layer has an active selection, only the selected points are used to build the statistics.
A categorical raster whose matching cells define the reference sample. Used only when the statistics source is Categorical raster.

param.name: cat_field
param.displayname: Category field (informational; cell values are used)

dialogReference.para: Informational only - the reference cells are selected by their numeric cell value, not by an attribute-table field.
The categorical raster cell value whose cells form the reference sample for the mean and covariance.
How the covariance matrix is inverted when an inverse covariance table is requested. This setting is ignored unless the Output inverse covariance matrix table is specified.

Standard (inverse): the ordinary matrix inverse. Fast and exact for well-conditioned data and the right choice in almost all cases. It fails if the covariance matrix is singular, which usually means a variable has no variance (all values identical) or two variables are perfectly correlated.

Pseudo-inverse (SVD): the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse computed by singular value decomposition. Use it when variables are strongly collinear or the covariance is near-singular: it returns a stable least-squares inverse instead of failing, though it can mask redundant variables.
The tool reports the covariance condition number; very large values indicate nearly collinear variables.

Output table for the mean vector (one row per variable), with the ordered variable list stored in its metadata. Together with the covariance table, this is what the Mahalanobis Raster and at Points tools read through their Existing tables source. Auto-named Mahalanobis_Means in the current workspace; clear the box if you do not want this table.

Output table for the covariance matrix, with the ordered variable list stored in its metadata. Together with the mean vector table, this is what the Mahalanobis Raster and at Points tools read through their Existing tables source. Auto-named Mahalanobis_Covariance in the current workspace; clear the box if you do not want this table.

Optional output table for the inverse covariance matrix, computed using the chosen inversion method. Not required to reuse the statistics (the consuming tools invert the covariance themselves); provided for inspection. Leave empty to skip it.
Optional output table for the correlation matrix, derived from the covariance. Useful for screening collinearity among the variables. Leave empty to skip it.

scriptExample.title: MahalanobisCovariance example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: This example computes the mean vector and covariance matrix from three rasters - elev_clip, slope_clip, and curvature - sampled at a point layer named Sample_Points_for_Mahal, then writes both tables to a geodatabase. Those two tables can then be passed to the Mahalanobis Raster or at Points tools as their Existing tables source.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages out_gdb = r"C:\Project\Mahalanobis.gdb" arcpy.jenness.MahalanobisCovariance( raster_vars="elev_clip;slope_clip;curvature", sample_method="Interpolated (bilinear)", stats_source="Calculate directly from sample point features", points="Sample_Points_for_Mahal", inversion="Standard (inverse)", out_mean=out_gdb + r"\Mahalanobis_Means", out_cov=out_gdb + r"\Mahalanobis_Covariance", out_invcov=out_gdb + r"\Mahalanobis_Inv_Covariance", out_corr=out_gdb + r"\Mahalanobis_Correlation")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Computes mean, covariance, inverse covariance, and correlation tables for a set of landscape variables, for reuse by the Mahalanobis distance tools.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Computes the multivariate statistics used by the Mahalanobis distance formula - the mean vector and covariance matrix, plus optionally the inverse covariance and correlation matrices - for a set of landscape variables, and writes them as tables. The statistics are derived from sample point features or from the cells of a categorical raster matching a chosen value. Landscape variables are supplied exactly as in the other Mahalanobis tools (rasters, with multiband rasters expanding to one variable per band, plus optional polygon variables rasterized from a numeric field). Each table embeds the ordered variable list in its metadata so the mean and covariance can be supplied to the Mahalanobis Raster or at Points tools through their Existing tables source, with the variable order validated. This is the producer tool of the Mahalanobis suite, letting the statistics be computed once and reused. Method reference: Mahalanobis (1936).
